name: ACC Eastview Campus
story: An ACC campus in East Austin off Webberville Road.
extra: The campus sits on the site of the old Anderson High School, the segregated Black high school that Austin closed in 1971 during court-ordered desegregation.

name: ACC Rio Grande Campus
story: ACC's original campus west of downtown, in a 1916 building that housed Austin High School from 1925 until 1975. ACC took it over that same year.
extra: It opened as Allan Junior High and swapped buildings with Austin High in 1925. A $49 million renovation reopened it in 2021, more than a century after it was built.

name: Austin Central Library
story: The six-storey central branch at Cesar Chavez and Shoal Creek, opened in 2017. Built to LEED Platinum with a rooftop garden and a reading porch over the creek.
extra: Named one of Time's World's Greatest Places the year it opened. Locals mostly use it as a place to sit rather than to borrow books.

name: Austin Convention Center
story: The downtown convention center on Cesar Chavez, opened in 1992 and expanded in 2002 to about 880,000 square feet.
extra: It is the main venue for SXSW every March. The city approved a full demolition and rebuild, closing it in 2025 for several years.
notes: Demolished Oct 2025; replacement opens 2029. Not a place you can visit.

name: Austin History Center
story: The city's archive downtown, in the 1933 building that was Austin's first purpose-built public library.
extra: The 1933 Italian Renaissance building was Austin's first purpose-built public library and served as the main branch until 1979. It is on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Austin Nature & Science Center
story: An eight-acre nature center in Zilker Park with live native animals and a dino pit.
extra: The Dino Pit is a real dig site where children uncover fossil casts moulded from actual specimens in the Texas Memorial Museum's collection. The Trade Counter lets kids bring in natural objects and trade them for points toward others.

name: Austin State Hospital
story: The state psychiatric hospital north of the UT campus, opened in 1861 as the Texas State Lunatic Asylum. It is the oldest psychiatric hospital in Texas and was the first built west of the Mississippi.
extra: The main building is the third-oldest standing public building in Texas. A 2022 construction dig on the grounds turned up 6,500 artifacts from its self-sufficient years, when it ran its own dairy farm, ice factory and tailor shop.

name: Blanton Museum of Art
story: One of the largest university art museums in the country, on the UT campus, holding more than 22,000 works.
extra: Ellsworth Kelly's 'Austin', a stone building with coloured glass he designed as a work of art in itself, stands on the grounds. It was his final work.

name: Concordia University Texas
story: A Lutheran university on a 400-acre campus in northwest Austin, moved here from Hyde Park in 2008.
extra: The 384-acre campus includes a 250-acre nature preserve with caves and wetlands, home to two endangered birds: the golden-cheeked warbler and the black-capped vireo. Concordia bought the land from Schlumberger and moved here from Hyde Park in 2008.

name: Dell Children's Medical Center
story: The region's children's hospital, in Mueller since 2007, built on the old airport grounds.
extra: It was the first hospital in the world to earn LEED Platinum certification, powered by its own on-site natural gas plant on the former airport grounds.

name: Dell Seton Medical Center
story: The teaching hospital for UT's Dell Medical School, opened downtown in 2017, replacing Brackenridge as the region's Level I trauma centre.
extra: It replaced Brackenridge, which opened in 1884 as the first public hospital in Texas and ran for 133 years. Dell Seton is the only Level I trauma centre in Central Texas, taking the worst cases from eleven counties.

name: Elisabet Ney Museum
story: The limestone studio of sculptor Elisabet Ney in Hyde Park, built in 1892 and a museum since 1911.
extra: Ney had already carved Schopenhauer and Bismarck in Europe before moving to Texas. Her statues of Austin and Houston stand in the Capitol.

name: French Legation
story: An 1841 house in East Austin built for the French chargé d'affaires to the Republic of Texas, the oldest surviving house in the city.
extra: The Pig War of 1841 started here, when the envoy's servants killed a neighbour's pigs that had got into his stables. Diplomatic relations broke off over it.

name: George Washington Carver Museum
story: A museum and cultural center in East Austin devoted to African American history and art, opened in 1980.
extra: It was the first neighborhood museum in Texas dedicated to Black history, housed at first in the original Austin public library building.

name: Harry Ransom Center
story: A humanities archive on the UT campus holding 42 million manuscript pages, a million rare books, and five million photographs.
extra: It owns a complete Gutenberg Bible and the world's first photograph, Niépce's 1826 view from a window in Burgundy.

name: Huston-Tillotson University
story: A historically Black university in East Austin, and the oldest institution of higher learning in the city. Tillotson opened in 1875, eight years before UT, and merged with Samuel Huston College in 1952.
extra: The 20-acre campus is on the National Register of Historic Places. Alumni include Frederick D. Patterson, who founded the United Negro College Fund, and Volma Overton, who led the fight to desegregate Austin schools.

osmTags.wikipedia: en:Lago Vista TX - Rusty Allen Airport

name: LBJ Presidential Library
story: The presidential library on the east side of the UT campus, opened in 1971, holding 45 million pages of Johnson's papers.
extra: There is a seven-eighths scale replica of the Oval Office on the top floor, and an animatronic LBJ that tells jokes.

name: Mexic-Arte Museum
story: Texas's official Mexican and Mexican American fine art museum, on Congress Avenue downtown, founded in 1984.
extra: Founded in 1984 by artists Sylvia Orozco, Sam Coronado and Pio Pulido. Its Día de los Muertos parade started that same year and is now the largest and longest-running in Texas.

name: Neill-Cochran House Museum
story: An 1856 Greek Revival house west of the UT campus, one of the oldest buildings in Austin.
extra: Its original slave quarters still stand, one of very few surviving in the city, and are now part of the museum's permanent exhibit.

name: O. Henry Museum
story: The 1891 cottage where William Sydney Porter lived, moved to Brush Square downtown.
extra: He wrote as O. Henry, a pen name he took up while serving a prison sentence for embezzlement from an Austin bank.

name: Perry-Castañeda Library
story: UT's main library, a brutalist block on the east side of campus holding about three million volumes.
extra: Seen from above the building is shaped like Texas, which was intentional.

name: Seminary of the Southwest
story: An Episcopal seminary just northeast of the UT campus, founded in 1951.
extra: Its Booher Library holds one of the largest theological collections in the Southwest, and the campus sits on land donated from the estate of a Texas cattle fortune.

name: Southwestern University
story: A private liberal arts college in Georgetown, and the oldest university in Texas. Its charter traces to Rutersville College, chartered by the Congress of the Republic of Texas in 1840.
extra: Four separate Methodist colleges were folded together to create it in 1873. Enrolment is about 1,500, roughly a thirtieth of UT's.

name: St. David's Medical Center
story: A large hospital in central Austin off 32nd Street, part of the St. David's system.
extra: The hospital grew out of a 1924 sanitarium and is named for St. David's Episcopal Church, which founded it. Its neonatal unit is one of the largest in Central Texas.

name: St. Edward's University
story: A 160-acre Catholic university on a hill in South Austin, founded in 1878 by the Congregation of Holy Cross.
extra: Its Main Building, finished in 1889 and rebuilt after an 1903 fire and a 1922 tornado, is visible from much of South Congress.

name: Texas Memorial Museum
story: The natural history museum on the UT campus, opened in 1936 for the Texas centennial.
extra: The Texas Pterosaur hanging in the entry hall has a 40-foot wingspan and was found in Big Bend, the largest flying creature ever discovered.

name: Texas Military Forces Museum
story: The Texas National Guard museum at Camp Mabry, covering Texas military history from 1823.
extra: Among its holdings is the field cap of Field Marshal Erwin Rommel, captured by the 36th Infantry Division in North Africa. The tank collection outside runs from a Sherman to an M1 Abrams, and several still run.

name: Texas State Archives
story: The state archive just east of the Capitol, holding Texas government records back to the Republic.
extra: Named for the first vice president of the Republic of Texas. The original Texas Declaration of Independence is kept here.

name: Bullock Texas State History Museum
story: The state history museum just north of the Capitol, opened in 2001. Three floors of exhibits plus an IMAX theater.
extra: The 35-foot bronze Lone Star out front weighs about six tons. Named for Bob Bullock, the lieutenant governor who pushed the museum through.

name: Texas State University
story: A 500-acre campus in San Marcos, south of the metro, with about 40,000 students.
extra: Lyndon Johnson graduated from here in 1930, the only US president educated in Texas.
notes: San Marcos, 47 km out and outside the camera box; best reachable guess scored 33.

name: The Contemporary Austin
story: A contemporary art museum on Congress Avenue downtown, one half of an institution that also runs Laguna Gloria on Lake Austin.
extra: The institution runs two sites: this one downtown and Laguna Gloria, a 1916 Italianate villa on a Lake Austin peninsula with a 14-acre sculpture park.

name: The Long Center for the Performing Arts

osmTags.wikipedia: en:Long Center for the Performing Arts

name: The Thinkery
story: Austin's children's museum, in Mueller since 2013. Formerly the Austin Children's Museum downtown.
extra: It began in 1983 as the Austin Children's Museum, with founders driving tabletop exhibits around town in a station wagon. A million-dollar gift from Michael and Susan Dell funded the move that eventually brought it to Mueller in 2013.

name: University of Texas at Austin
story: The 431-acre flagship campus just north of the Capitol, opened in 1883 with one building and 221 students. Now around 53,000 students, one of the largest universities in the country.
extra: The Tower, the Blanton, the Ransom Center and DKR Stadium all sit inside these grounds. The land was funded by 2.1 million acres of West Texas the state set aside in 1876, which turned out to be sitting on oil.

name: Antone's Nightclub
story: Austin's home of the blues, founded by Clifford Antone in 1975 and now on East Fifth Street after several moves.
extra: Antone booked Muddy Waters, Buddy Guy and Albert King, and a teenage Stevie Ray Vaughan played the house band here before anyone outside Austin knew his name.

name: Barley Swine
story: A tasting-menu restaurant in North Austin from the same team as Odd Duck.
extra: It started in 2010 in a 48-seat room on South Lamar with no reservations and a line down the block, then moved north for space.

name: Cactus Cafe
story: A 200-seat listening room inside the UT student union, running since 1979.
extra: Lyle Lovett, Nanci Griffith and Robert Earl Keen all built early followings here. The room enforces silence during songs, which is rare enough in Austin to be its whole reputation.

name: Chili's (North Lamar)
story: A Chili's on North Lamar near 45th Street, an ordinary outpost of a chain that is unusually woven into Austin life.
extra: Chili's began in Dallas in 1975, and this location has outlasted most of the independent restaurants that opened around it.

name: Cisco's
story: A Mexican bakery and diner on East Sixth Street, open since 1950.
extra: Rudy Cisneros ran it as an unofficial political clubhouse; Lyndon Johnson and generations of Texas legislators held court in the back room over migas.

name: County Line on the Lake
story: A barbecue restaurant on Bull Creek at Lake Austin, in a building that was a 1920s roadhouse and speakeasy.
extra: Diners can arrive by boat, and the deck over the water is the reason most people come.

name: Curra's Grill
story: An interior Mexican restaurant on Oltorf in South Austin, open since 1994.
extra: Its avocado margarita is widely credited as the first in Austin, and now appears on menus across the city.

name: Dirty Martin's Place
story: A hamburger stand on Guadalupe near campus, open since 1926 and still cooking on a griddle in the same building.
extra: It was called Dirty's because the original floor was dirt. A highway widening project has threatened the building for years.

name: El Chile Cafe y Cantina
story: An interior Mexican restaurant on Manor Road, part of the strip that made that street a dining destination in the 2000s.
extra: Manor Road was a quiet residential street until a handful of restaurants like this one opened along it in the early 2000s and turned it into one of Austin's denser dining strips.

name: Elysium
story: A Red River nightclub known for its goth and industrial nights, open since 2001.
extra: It has hosted the city's goth scene for more than two decades, with a sunken dance floor and themed nights that have outlasted most of the Red River strip around it.

name: Fonda San Miguel
story: An interior Mexican restaurant in North Loop, open since 1975 in a hacienda-style building full of Mexican art.
extra: It was among the first restaurants in the United States to serve regional Mexican cooking rather than Tex-Mex, and its Sunday brunch buffet has run for decades.

name: Franklin Barbecue
story: A barbecue joint on East 11th Street that opened as a trailer in 2009 and moved into this building in 2011.
extra: Aaron Franklin won a James Beard award in 2015, the first for a barbecue cook. The line used to start before dawn and regularly ran out of brisket by early afternoon.

name: Green Mesquite BBQ
story: A barbecue restaurant on Barton Springs Road, open since 1988.
extra: It sits on the strip near Zilker that has fed Austin City Limits crowds for decades.

name: Guero's Taco Bar
story: A Tex-Mex restaurant on South Congress in a building that was a feed and seed store from the 1920s.
extra: Bill Clinton ate here in 1996 and the booth is still pointed out. The backyard stage hosts free shows most weekends.

name: Historic Scoot Inn
story: A beer garden and music venue in East Austin, in a building that has served drinks since 1871.
extra: It is one of the oldest continuously operating bars in Texas, having run as a saloon for railroad workers long before East Austin was part of the city.

name: Home Slice Pizza
story: A New York style pizzeria on South Congress, open since 2005.
extra: It runs an annual pizza-tossing competition and its team has sent members to the world championships in Italy.

name: Hotel Vegas
story: A music venue on East Sixth Street with two stages and a patio between them.
extra: It anchors the East Sixth strip that replaced Red River as the centre of Austin's small-club scene through the 2010s.

name: Hut's Hamburgers
story: A burger restaurant on West Sixth Street, tracing to a stand opened in 1939.
extra: It closed in 2021 after 82 years, then reopened under new ownership, which makes it both one of the oldest restaurants in Austin and one of the newest.

name: Juan in a Million
story: A Mexican diner on East Cesar Chavez, open since 1980 and known for breakfast tacos.
extra: The Don Juan taco is large enough that finishing one is a minor local achievement. Anthony Bourdain filmed here.

name: Kerbey Lane Cafe (original)
story: The first Kerbey Lane, opened in 1980 in a converted house on Kerbey Lane in Rosedale.
extra: The pancakes and queso built a local chain now at half a dozen locations, but this bungalow is the one the name comes from.

name: Magnolia Cafe
story: A 24-hour diner on South Congress, open since 1979 and known for gingerbread pancakes and queso.
extra: Its slogan, sorry we're open, ran on a neon sign for decades. The original Lake Austin Boulevard location closed in 2020, leaving this one.

name: Matt's El Rancho
story: A Tex-Mex restaurant on South Lamar, opened by Matt Martinez in 1952 and still run by the family.
extra: The Bob Armstrong dip, queso with guacamole and taco meat, was invented here for a land commissioner who asked for something off-menu. It is now on Tex-Mex menus statewide.

name: Mohawk
story: A two-storey Red River venue with an outdoor stage, opened in 2006.
extra: The outdoor stage backs onto a limestone cliff, and the balconies looking down on it make it one of the best-sounding small rooms in the city.

name: Odd Duck
story: A South Lamar restaurant built around Texas farm ingredients, opened as a brick-and-mortar in 2013.
extra: It began in 2009 as a food trailer parked on the same lot, one of the first trailers in Austin taken seriously as a restaurant.

name: Oilcan Harry's
story: A Fourth Street bar opened in 1990, the anchor of Austin's Warehouse District gay scene.
extra: It is the oldest queer bar in Austin, opened by Larry Davis and still gay-owned, running drag, karaoke and bingo nights more than thirty years on.

name: Red Ash
story: An Italian restaurant on Colorado Street downtown, cooking over a wood-fired grill.
extra: The pasta is made in-house daily and the grill burns oak, which is where the name comes from.

name: Sandy's Hamburgers
story: A walk-up burger and frozen custard stand on Barton Springs Road, open since 1946.
extra: It is one of the last drive-in style stands left in central Austin, and the lot it sits on has been the subject of development fights for years.

name: Suerte
story: An East Austin restaurant on East Sixth focused on Oaxacan cooking and house-made masa.
extra: It nixtamalizes its own corn in-house, which almost no Austin restaurant did before it opened in 2018.

name: Terry Black's BBQ
story: A barbecue hall on Barton Springs Road run by the fourth generation of the Black family of Lockhart.
extra: The family has been smoking meat in Texas since 1932. A cousin runs a rival Black's in Lockhart, and the split has been the subject of more than one long magazine feature.

name: The Continental Club
story: A South Congress music room open since 1955, one of the oldest continuously operating venues in Austin.
extra: It started as a private supper club, became a burlesque house, and has run as a music venue since the 1970s. The neon sign out front is a South Congress landmark.

name: The Salt Lick BBQ
story: A barbecue restaurant in Driftwood, southwest of Austin, cooking over an open pit in the middle of the dining room since 1967.
extra: It is in a dry precinct, so it has never sold alcohol and diners bring their own. The original pit is still the one in use.

name: Torchy's Tacos (South Congress)
story: The South Congress Torchy's, the first permanent location of a taco chain that started as a trailer in 2006.
extra: It grew from one trailer to more than a hundred locations across several states. The Trailer Park taco, fried chicken with green chile queso, is the one that built it.

name: Uchi
story: A Japanese restaurant on South Lamar in a converted 1930s bungalow, opened by Tyson Cole in 2003.
extra: Cole won a James Beard award in 2011, and Uchi is widely credited with changing what Austin expected from a restaurant. Its alumni run kitchens across the city.

name: Uchiko
story: The North Lamar sibling to Uchi, opened in 2010.
extra: Its name means child of Uchi. Chef Paul Qui won Top Chef while running the kitchen here.

name: Airmen's Cave
story: A cave entrance in the Barton Creek Greenbelt, leading to a passage more than two miles long.
extra: At about 11,300 feet it is one of the longest caves in Texas, and almost all of it is tight crawlway. It once fed Barton Springs before the water table dropped.

name: Ann W. Richards Congress Avenue Bridge
story: Carries Congress Avenue over Lady Bird Lake, renamed in 2006 for Ann Richards, the 45th governor of Texas and a longtime Austin resident. A concrete arch bridge with six lanes.
extra: The 1980 renovation left expansion joints that turned out to be ideal bat roosts. About 1.5 million Mexican free-tailed bats now live underneath, the largest urban bat colony in North America, and the evening emergence draws crowds all summer.

name: Austin by Ellsworth Kelly
story: A stone building with coloured glass windows on the Blanton Museum grounds, designed by Ellsworth Kelly as a work of art rather than a gallery.
extra: It was his final work, designed in 1986 and not built until 2018, after his death. Kelly never saw it completed.

name: Barbara Jordan Statue
story: A bronze of Barbara Jordan on the UT campus, installed in 2009 near the student union.

osmTags.wikipedia: en:Statue of Barbara Jordan (University of Texas at Austin)

extra: Jordan was the first Black woman elected to Congress from the South, and she taught at UT's LBJ School for seventeen years after leaving Washington.

name: Barton Springs Pool
story: A three-acre swimming pool fed entirely by underground springs, sitting in the channel of Barton Creek inside Zilker Park. Main Barton Spring is the fourth-largest in Texas and pushes water out at a steady 68 to 74 degrees year-round.
extra: That constant temperature means people swim it in January. It is also home to the Barton Springs salamander, which lives nowhere else on Earth.

name: Deep Eddy Pool
story: The oldest swimming pool in Texas, spring-fed and concrete-lined, opened as a resort in 1915 on the north bank of the Colorado.
extra: The original owner drew crowds with a Ferris wheel and a diving horse. The city bought it in 1935 and the WPA rebuilt the bathhouse you see today.

name: Eliza Spring
story: A small spring-fed pool just downstream of Barton Springs, one of the four springs in the Barton Springs complex.
extra: It holds one of the largest populations of the Barton Springs salamander, a species that lives nowhere else on Earth.

name: Goddess of Liberty
story: The original zinc statue that stood atop the Capitol dome from 1888 until 1985, now displayed at ground level on the Capitol grounds.
extra: She is nearly sixteen feet tall and was sculpted with exaggerated features so she would read correctly from 300 feet below. A replica took her place on the dome.

name: Henry G. Madison Cabin
story: A log cabin built around 1863 by Henry Green Madison, now standing in Rosewood Park.
extra: Madison was Austin's first African American city council member. He built a larger house around the cabin in the 1880s, hiding it until a demolition crew found it in the 1960s. It was moved to Rosewood Park in 1973 and restored again in 2026.

name: Kenney-Lomax House
story: A 19th-century house east of downtown, associated with folklorist John Lomax.
extra: Lomax and his son Alan recorded thousands of American folk songs for the Library of Congress, including the first recordings of Lead Belly.

name: Lamar Boulevard Bridge
story: The Lamar Boulevard bridge over Lady Bird Lake, opened in 1942 and widened since.
extra: The pedestrian bridge alongside it carries the hike-and-bike trail and gives the clearest downtown skyline view of any crossing.

name: Martin Luther King Jr. Statue
story: A bronze of Dr. King on the UT campus at the East Mall, installed in 1999.
extra: It was the first statue of King on a major Southern university campus, and student campaigns had pushed for it for more than a decade.

name: Mather-Kirkland House
story: A 19th-century house in East Austin, one of the few of its era surviving on that side of I-35.
extra: It is one of the Austin houses individually listed on the National Register, a designation only a handful of 19th-century residences here have earned.

name: Michael Paggi House
story: An 1870s house near downtown built for Michael Paggi, an Italian immigrant carriage maker.
extra: Paggi brought the first ice-making machine to Austin, and his carriage works stood on the site where the Paggi House restaurant later operated.

name: Moonlight Tower (Canterbury St & Lynn St)
story: One of Austin's moonlight towers, cast-iron lamp towers 165 feet tall that have lit the city since 1895. Austin bought 31 secondhand from Detroit in 1894; seventeen survive.
extra: They are the only moonlight towers left standing anywhere in the world. Each threw enough light to read a watch by within a 1,500-foot circle, and all seventeen are on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Mount Bonnell
story: At roughly 780 feet, the highest easily reachable point in Austin, overlooking Lake Austin from a limestone bluff. About a hundred stone steps get you to the top.
extra: It has been a tourist destination since the 1850s, which makes it one of the oldest attractions in the city. The tradition says a couple who climbs it together will fall in love.

name: Pennybacker Bridge
story: The Percy V. Pennybacker Jr. Bridge, carrying Loop 360 across Lake Austin. A through-arch design in weathering steel, which is why it wears that rust color on purpose.
extra: The arch was assembled on the bank and floated into place on barges. The cliff on the south side is one of the most photographed overlooks in the city.

osmTags.wikipedia: en:James D. Pfluger Pedestrian and Bicycle Bridge

name: Pilot Knob
story: A low hill southeast of Austin near McKinney Falls, the eroded core of an extinct volcano.
extra: It erupted underwater about 80 million years ago, when this part of Texas was ocean floor. It is the most prominent of several volcanic remnants around Austin.

name: Seiders Springs
story: Springs along Shoal Creek north of 34th Street, feeding the creek year-round.
extra: Edward Seiders ran a bathhouse and picnic resort here in the 1870s. Stone steps from it are still visible on the creek bank.

name: Sheeks-Robertson House
story: An 1897 house at Sixth Street and West Lynn in Old West Austin.
extra: It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1976, one of a cluster of surviving Victorian houses on the near west side.

name: Stevie Ray Vaughan Statue
story: A bronze of the Austin blues guitarist on the Lady Bird Lake hike-and-bike trail at Auditorium Shores, installed in 1993, less than three years after he died in a helicopter crash.
extra: Sculptor Ralph Helmick posed him with his hat and a long shadow cast behind. It was the first statue in Austin honoring a musician.

name: Swedish Log Cabin
story: An 1840s log cabin moved to Zilker Park, built by one of the Swedish families who settled east of Austin.
extra: Swedish immigrants founded the Govalle area in the 1850s, and the name comes from the Swedish for good pasture.

name: Texas Peace Officers Memorial
story: A memorial on the Capitol grounds honouring Texas law enforcement officers killed in the line of duty, dedicated in 1999.
extra: Designed by Linda Johnson and erected in 1999, it is a granite obelisk with the names of officers killed since 1823, when Stephen F. Austin commissioned the first Texas peace officers.

name: Texas State Capitol
story: Finished in 1888 and built from Texas pink granite hauled in from Marble Falls on a railroad laid specifically for the job. Elijah Myers designed it, and at 302 feet the dome stands taller than the US Capitol, a fact Texans mention roughly every chance they get.
extra: The state paid for it in land, not money: the builders took three million acres of the Panhandle instead of cash, which became the XIT Ranch.

name: The Driskill
story: The oldest operating hotel in Austin, a Romanesque pile finished in 1886 at Sixth and Brazos. Cattleman Jesse Driskill built it, intending 'the finest hotel south of St. Louis'.
extra: He lost it in a poker game within two years. Lyndon and Lady Bird Johnson had their first date in the dining room, and LBJ later watched election returns from a suite upstairs.

name: Third Street Railroad Trestle
story: A steel railroad trestle over Shoal Creek downtown, part of the line that has run through Austin since the 1870s.
extra: It carries the line that made Austin a rail town in 1871, when the Houston and Texas Central finally reached the city and ended its isolation.

name: UT Tower
story: The Main Building at the center of the UT campus, finished in 1937. Its 307-foot tower runs 27 floors and is visible from most of central Austin.
extra: It gets lit burnt orange for wins, and fully orange with a lit-up number one for a national championship. Locals read the tower the way you would read a scoreboard.

name: Wahrenberger House
story: An 1868 Classical Revival house two blocks north of the Capitol on West 14th Street.
extra: Built by Friedrich Huster and deeded in 1882 to Caroline Wahrenberger, whose name it carries. It is on the National Register and a Recorded Texas Historic Landmark.

name: Whirlpool Cave
story: A cave in southwest Austin, one of the karst features formed in the Edwards limestone that underlies the aquifer.
extra: It has the largest single room of any cave in Travis County, and at about 1,440 feet of passage it is a standard training trip for Austin caving groups.

name: Willie Nelson Statue
story: An eight-foot bronze of Willie Nelson at Second and Lavaca, outside ACL Live at the Moody Theater. Sculpted by Clete Shields for Capital Area Statues.
extra: It was unveiled on April 20, 2011, at 4:20 in the afternoon. Nobody involved has ever claimed that was a coincidence.

name: Allandale
story: North central Austin, known for big lots and mature trees, roughly between Burnet, Shoal Creek, 2222 and Anderson. Developed in the 1950s.
extra: It is one of the largest contiguous mid-century neighborhoods in the city, which is why so much of it still looks like 1958.

name: Barton Hills
story: A hillside neighborhood in 78704, wedged between the Barton Creek Greenbelt and Zilker Park. Built out mostly in the 1950s and 60s on lots that step down toward the creek.
extra: Barton Hills Elementary sits at the center, and the greenbelt trailheads at the end of several residential streets are the reason people live there.

name: Bouldin Creek
story: Just south of the river between South First and South Congress, platted around 1900 and built out through the 1920s and 30s. One of the closest neighborhoods to downtown.
extra: Named for James Bouldin, whose land it was. The creek still runs through it, mostly buried.

name: Brentwood
story: Central north Austin between Lamar and Burnet, around Justin and Arroyo Seco. Postwar houses on a regular grid.
extra: Brentwood Park and the neighborhood pool are the center of it, and it shares a school and an identity with Crestview next door.

name: Chestnut
story: East Austin between Manor Road and MLK, around Chestnut Avenue. A historically Black neighborhood built out in the early 20th century.
extra: Like much of East Austin, it was shaped by the 1928 city plan that pushed Black residents east of East Avenue, now I-35.

name: Coronado Hills
story: Northeast Austin off Cameron Road near US 290, a small 1960s subdivision.
extra: A compact 1960s subdivision built when Cameron Road was still the edge of town, and one of the first parts of northeast Austin developed after the airport opened nearby.

name: Crestview
story: North central, just east of Burnet Road around Justin Lane and Woodrow. A postwar subdivision built for returning GIs in the late 1940s and 50s.
extra: The Crestview Minimax sign on Woodrow is a neighborhood landmark, kept when the grocery underneath it closed.

name: Dawson
story: South Austin bounded by Oltorf, Ben White, South First and Congress. Small postwar houses.
extra: Named for the Dawson Massacre of 1842, by way of the elementary school.

name: Galindo
story: South Austin in 78704, west of South First around Mary Street and Oltorf.
extra: Named for the Galindo family, whose farm the subdivision was cut from in the 1930s.

name: Garrison Park
story: Southwest Austin in 78745 around Garrison Park and William Cannon.
extra: The neighbourhood and the district park share a name but not a boundary; the park is formally James A. Garrison District Park and sits at its southern edge.

name: Georgian Acres
story: North Austin between I-35 and Lamar around Rundberg Lane.
extra: The Rundberg corridor running through it has one of the highest concentrations of immigrant-owned small businesses in Austin.

name: Govalle
story: East Austin along the river between Pleasant Valley and Springdale. Named from the Swedish 'go valla', meaning good pasture.
extra: Swedish immigrant Svante Palm named his farm here in the 1850s. Govalle Park and the elementary school keep the name.

name: Hancock
story: North central, ZIP 78751 and 78705, just northeast of the UT campus around 41st and Duval.
extra: Home to Hancock Golf Course, the oldest course in Texas, opened in 1899 and still only nine holes.

name: Heritage Hills
story: Northeast Austin near Cameron Road and US 290, next to Windsor Hills.
extra: Built out in the 1960s alongside Windsor Hills next door, the two are often confused even by people who live in them.

name: Highland
story: Northeast of central Austin around Airport Boulevard and I-35, near the old Highland Mall.
extra: Highland Mall was Austin's first enclosed mall, opened in 1971. It closed in 2015 and is now Austin Community College's Highland campus.

name: Holly
story: East of I-35 along the south bank of the river, around Holly Street. A largely Mexican American neighborhood since the mid 20th century.
extra: The Holly Street Power Plant sat here from 1960 until 2007. Neighbors fought for decades to close it; the land is now parkland.

name: Hyde Park
story: Austin's first planned suburb, laid out in 1891 by Monroe Shipe between 38th and 45th, Duval and Guadalupe. Shipe ran his own streetcar line down Speedway to sell the lots.
extra: The Elisabet Ney Museum sits inside it, and Shipe's original marketing promised the neighborhood would be 'exclusively for white residents' - a deed restriction Austin spent the next century unwinding.

name: Johnston Terrace
story: East Austin near the old Johnston High School, between Govalle and the river.
extra: The school opened in 1960 and was closed by the state in 2008 for low performance, reopening as Eastside Memorial.

name: Montopolis
story: Southeast Austin south of the river in 78741, bounded by Lady Bird Lake, Grove Street and US 183. One of the oldest settled areas in Travis County.
extra: There were two Montopolises: the first, north of the river during the Republic of Texas, and today's neighborhood south of it.

name: Mueller
story: A 700-acre planned neighborhood on the site of Robert Mueller Municipal Airport, which was Austin's airport until it closed in 1999. Redevelopment began in 2007.
extra: The old air traffic control tower still stands and is a protected landmark. Streets in the neighborhood are named for aviation figures.

name: North Burnet
story: Northwest Austin, a 2,300 acre district bounded by Walnut Creek, US 183, Metric and MoPac. Austin's designated second downtown.
extra: The Domain and Q2 Stadium both sit inside it, and the city's plan calls for it to hold far more housing than it does today.

name: North Lamar
story: North Austin along North Lamar Boulevard above US 183.
extra: The stretch through it has one of the densest concentrations of Vietnamese and Korean businesses in the city.

name: North Loop
story: North central along North Loop Boulevard between Lamar and Duval. A small strip of vintage shops, record stores and bungalows.
extra: The street was literally the northern loop of the city limits when it was named.

name: North University
story: Directly north of the UT campus, between Guadalupe and Duval, roughly 26th to 38th. A mix of old houses cut into apartments and newer student towers.
extra: The blocks here were platted in the 1890s as UT expanded north, and several of the surviving houses are among the oldest continuously occupied homes near campus.

name: Oak Hill
story: Southwest Austin where US 290 and TX 71 split, an unincorporated community and a collection of neighborhoods annexed piecemeal over decades.
sourceRef: WEST OAK HILL + EAST OAK HILL
extra: The intersection is known locally as the Y at Oak Hill, and it has been the subject of highway redesign fights for more than thirty years.

name: Old Enfield
story: West of downtown between Lamar and MoPac, north of the river. Austin's wealthiest early streetcar suburb, developed in the 1910s and 20s.
extra: It takes its name from the Enfield plantation that once covered the land, and Pease Park runs along its eastern edge.

name: Old West Austin
story: West of Lamar and north of the river, taking in Clarksville and part of Enfield. One of the oldest continuously settled parts of the city.
extra: Clarksville within it was founded in 1871 by Charles Clark, a freedman, and is one of the oldest surviving freedom colonies west of the Mississippi.

name: Pecan Springs-Springdale
story: East Austin around Springdale Road and Manor Road, north of Govalle.
extra: Pecan Springs was a separate rural settlement before Austin grew out to meet it.

name: Pleasant Valley
story: Southeast Austin east of I-35 along Pleasant Valley Road, south of the river.
extra: The name comes from Pleasant Valley Road, which follows an old river-bottom farm route along the Colorado before the lakes were dammed.

name: Riverside
story: South of Lady Bird Lake along East Riverside Drive, running east toward Pleasant Valley. Dense apartment blocks built through the 1970s and 80s.
extra: It has long been where a large share of UT and ACC students actually live, and is now the front line of Austin's redevelopment fights.

name: RMMA
story: Robert Mueller Municipal Airport, Austin's airport from 1930 until 1999, now redeveloped as the Mueller neighborhood in East Austin.
extra: The old air traffic control tower still stands as a protected landmark, and neighborhood streets are named for aviation figures.

name: Rosedale
story: North central, bounded by 38th, Shoal Creek, Hancock Drive and Lamar. Small 1930s and 40s houses on a tight grid.
extra: Ramsey Park and the Seton hospital campus anchor opposite ends of it.

name: Rosewood
story: East Austin around Rosewood Avenue, north of 12th Street. The historic heart of Black Austin, with Rosewood Park at its center.
extra: The park opened in 1929 as the city's park for Black residents during segregation, and still hosts Juneteenth celebrations.

name: South Manchaca
story: South Austin along Manchaca Road, southwest of Ben White.
extra: The road is spelled Manchaca but pronounced MAN-shack, after Jose Antonio Menchaca. The town of the same name renamed itself Menchaca in 2018; Austin's road did not.

name: South River City
story: South of the river below downtown, in 78704. The planning area that contains Travis Heights, which is what almost everyone actually calls it.
extra: Stacy Park and its spring-fed pool run down the middle, and the Travis Heights hills give some of the best downtown views in the city.

name: St Edwards
story: South Austin around St. Edward's University, between Congress and I-35 north of Ben White.
extra: The university's Main Building, finished in 1889, sits on the hill and is visible from much of South Congress.

name: St John
story: North central Austin around St. Johns Avenue and I-35, north of Highland.
extra: Named for the St. John Regular Baptist Association, which ran an orphanage and encampment grounds on the site from 1907.

name: Sweetbriar
story: South Austin west of Congress around Sweetbriar Avenue and Ben White.
extra: A small postwar subdivision west of Congress, laid out with curving streets at a time when most of South Austin was still on a strict grid.

name: University Hills
story: Northeast Austin east of I-35 near the old Mueller airport approach, developed in the 1960s.
extra: It was one of the first Austin subdivisions marketed to Black professional families after the end of legal segregation.

name: Upper Boggy Creek
story: East central Austin around Boggy Creek, roughly between Manor Road, Airport and the cemetery. Includes the Cherrywood area.
extra: Patterson Park and the creek greenbelt run through it, and Manor Road's restaurant strip is its commercial edge.

name: West University
story: The blocks immediately west of the UT campus, between Guadalupe and Lamar north of 21st. Almost entirely student housing.
extra: The Drag runs along its eastern edge, and the neighborhood's density is why UT students can live without a car.

name: Westgate
story: Southwest Austin in 78745, near the Westgate shopping center off Ben White.
extra: Named for the Westgate shopping centre off Ben White, which opened in the 1960s as one of the first suburban retail centres south of the river.

name: Windsor Hills
story: Northeast Austin north of US 290 near Cameron Road, distinct from Windsor Park to the south.
extra: Distinct from Windsor Park to the south, a confusion that predates both: the names came from the same developer marketing separate tracts a few years apart.

name: Windsor Park
story: Northeast Austin bounded roughly by 51st, Manor Road, US 290 and I-35. A large 1950s subdivision.
extra: Bartholomew Park and its pool are the center of it, and Mueller sits just to the south.

name: Wooten
story: North central Austin bounded by Burnet Road, Anderson Lane and US 183, bisected by Ohlen Road.
extra: Named for the Wooten family, whose farm covered this land before Burnet Road was paved. Ohlen Road, which splits the neighbourhood, follows the old farm boundary.

name: Zilker
story: South of Lady Bird Lake, bounded roughly by Barton Skyway, the Union Pacific line, and Azie Morton. Named for Andrew Zilker, who donated the park land to the city in 1917.
extra: The neighborhood and the park share a name but not a boundary. Locals mean the park; the planning area is the houses east of it.

name: Adams-Hemphill Neighborhood Park
story: Eleven acres northwest of the UT campus along Waller Creek, between Duval and Red River.
extra: Waller Creek runs the length of it, and the park is one of the few green corridors linking the UT campus north toward Hyde Park.

name: Auditorium Shores
story: The park on the south bank of Lady Bird Lake, officially Vic Mathias Shores since 2017 though almost nobody calls it that. Best known for its skyline view and the off-leash dog area.
extra: The Stevie Ray Vaughan statue stands here, and the lawn has been a concert ground since the 1970s.

name: Auditorium Shores at Town Lake Metropolitan Park
Balcones District Park
story: Fifty-six acres in northwest Austin off Amherst Drive, with a pool and recreation center.
extra: It sits along the Balcones Escarpment, the fault line that splits Austin between Hill Country limestone to the west and blackland prairie to the east.

name: Bartholomew District Park
story: Fifty-two acres in Windsor Park off 51st Street, with a pool, disc golf, and trails.
extra: Its pool has been a neighbourhood fixture since the 1960s and is one of the largest in the city system, long enough that swim teams train in it.

name: Barton Creek Greenbelt
story: A 465-acre corridor following Barton Creek from Zilker southwest toward MoPac and beyond. Roughly seven miles of trail with limestone cliffs and seasonal swimming holes.
extra: Campbell's Hole, Twin Falls, and Sculpture Falls only hold water when the creek is running, which is why locals check the flow gauge before driving out.

name: Bee Cave Central Park
story: Forty-five acres in Bee Cave west of Austin, with trails through the Hill Country scrub.
extra: The park backs onto Hill Country scrub that is prime golden-cheeked warbler habitat, which shaped how much of it could be developed.

name: Big Stacy Neighborhood Park
story: Five acres in Travis Heights along Blunn Creek, with a spring-fed pool at the south end.
extra: The pool runs about 70 degrees year-round from the same aquifer that feeds Barton Springs, and it is heated in winter.

name: Blunn Creek Greenbelt
story: A twelve-acre creek corridor in South Austin below Travis Heights, running toward Little Stacy Park.
extra: The Blunn Creek Nature Preserve just south of it has a volcanic outcrop, the remains of a Cretaceous underwater volcano.

name: Boggy Creek Greenbelt
story: Fifty-six acres following Boggy Creek through East Austin, connecting Rosewood to the Colorado River.
extra: The creek was straightened and channelled in the mid-20th century after repeated flooding; recent city work has been undoing that, letting it meander again.

name: Bright Leaf Natural Area
story: 216 acres of preserved Hill Country in west Austin off 2222, left to the city by Georgia Lucas on the condition it stay undeveloped.
extra: It is open only on guided hikes, which is why most Austinites have never been inside despite driving past it constantly.

name: Brush Square
story: One of the four original 1839 squares, at Fifth and Neches downtown. Home to the O. Henry Museum and the Austin Fire Museum.
extra: O. Henry lived in the cottage here in the 1890s, before the embezzlement conviction that sent him to prison, where he started writing seriously.

name: Bull Creek District Park
story: Fifty-five acres in northwest Austin where Bull Creek runs over limestone shelves, with swimming holes and a waterfall upstream.
extra: Bull Creek runs over limestone shelves here, forming shallow pools that hold water even in dry summers. A waterfall sits a short walk upstream.

name: Butler Park
story: Twenty-two acres on the south shore of Lady Bird Lake, across from downtown. Known for the hill, the fountain, and the best skyline view in the city.
extra: The Liz Carpenter Fountain is a splash pad in summer. The hill was built from fill dredged out of the lake.

name: Circle C Metropolitan Park
story: 190 acres in southwest Austin along Slaughter Creek, serving the Circle C Ranch area.
extra: The land came to the city as part of the Circle C Ranch development agreement, one of the largest water-quality land deals in Austin's history over the Edwards Aquifer.

name: Commons Ford Ranch Metropolitan Park
story: 215 acres on Lake Austin west of the city, a former ranch with restored prairie and a long shoreline.
extra: The prairie restoration made it one of the best birding spots in Travis County.

name: Dave Reed Park
story: Ten acres in Cedar Park north of Austin.
extra: Cedar Park was a rail stop called Running Brushy until 1887; the park is part of the small civic core that grew up around the depot.

name: Dick Nichols District Park
story: 104 acres in southwest Austin off Beckett Road, with a pool, trails, and ballfields.
extra: The Latta Branch Greenbelt runs through it, one of the few creek corridors in far southwest Austin left undeveloped as the area filled in during the 1980s.

name: Dottie Jordan Park
story: Seven acres in Windsor Park off Loyola Lane, with a pool and recreation center.
extra: Dottie Jordan was an AISD orchestra teacher who lived across the street and asked the city council in 1972 to preserve park land here. She died the next year at 32; the city bought the 11.5 acres months later and named it for her.

name: Dove Springs District Park
story: Fifty-seven acres in southeast Austin off Ainez Drive, serving the Dove Springs neighborhood.
extra: Dove Springs flooded catastrophically in 2013 and 2015 when Onion Creek rose; the park and its recreation centre served as the neighbourhood's emergency shelter both times.

name: Eastwoods Neighborhood Park
story: Ten acres northeast of the UT campus in the Hancock area, with a pool and a creek running through a wooded ravine.
extra: The wooded ravine through the middle is a remnant of the creek bottom that once ran open across this whole part of central Austin before it was culverted.

name: Festival Beach
story: Eighty acres on the south shore of the river east of I-35, officially Edward Rendon Sr. Metropolitan Park. Fields, a hike-and-bike trail, and a community garden.
extra: Named for Edward Rendon Sr., an East Austin community organizer. Most people just call it Festival Beach.

name: Fiesta Gardens
story: Three acres on the south bank of the river east of I-35, the traditional venue for Austin's Cinco de Mayo and Diez y Seis celebrations.
extra: The Austin Reggae Festival and the Pachanga Latino Music Festival both run here.

name: Givens District Park
story: Twenty-eight acres in East Austin off Springdale, one of the largest parks on the east side.
extra: Named for Everett Givens, a dentist and civil rights advocate who spent decades pressing the city for equal services in East Austin.

name: Govalle Neighborhood Park
story: Twenty-six acres in East Austin along Boggy Creek, next to the neighborhood of the same name.
extra: Govalle takes its name from the Swedish go valla, good pasture, after Svante Palm's farm here in the 1850s. The park still follows the low ground along Boggy Creek.

name: Gus Garcia Park
story: Forty-seven acres in north Austin off Rundberg, with a recreation center and pool.
extra: Named for Gustavo Garcia, the civil rights lawyer who argued Hernandez v. Texas before the Supreme Court in 1954 and won Mexican Americans protection under the 14th Amendment.

name: James A. Garrison District Park
story: Forty-one acres in southwest Austin off Manchaca Road, with a pool and ballfields.
extra: The park is one of the largest green spaces in 78745, a ZIP code that grew faster than almost any other part of Austin in the 1970s and 80s.

name: Little Stacy Neighborhood Park
story: Four acres in Travis Heights just north of Big Stacy, connected by the Blunn Creek trail.
extra: Blunn Creek runs between Little Stacy and Big Stacy just south of it; the trail connecting the two is a Travis Heights shortcut locals have used for generations.

name: Mabel Davis District Park
story: Sixty acres in southeast Austin off Burleson Road, with a pool and skate park.
extra: Mabel Davis led Austin's Red Cross volunteers in the Second World War and presided over the Violet Crown Garden Club and the Humane Society. The rose garden at Zilker's Botanical Garden carries her name too.

name: Mary Moore Searight Metropolitan Park
story: 334 acres in far south Austin off Slaughter Lane, with trails, disc golf, and a horse arena.
extra: Mary Moore Searight donated the family farm to the city in 1988 on the condition it stay parkland.

name: Metz Park
story: Seven acres in East Austin off Canterbury Street, with a pool and recreation center.
extra: The park has served this stretch of East Austin since 1914, one of the oldest continuously operating city parks on the east side.

name: Mueller Lake Park
story: Thirty-five acres at the center of the Mueller development, built on the old airport grounds. The lake is stormwater detention doing double duty.
extra: The old air traffic control tower still stands at the edge of the park, kept as a landmark when the airport closed in 1999.

name: Northwest District Park
story: Twenty-nine acres in north central Austin off Shoal Creek Boulevard, officially the Beverly S. Sheffield Northwest District Park.
extra: Sheffield ran Austin's parks department for decades and fought to keep Barton Springs free and open.

name: Old Settlers Park
story: 511 acres in Round Rock off US 79, one of the largest municipal parks in Central Texas. Built around baseball and softball complexes.
extra: The Dell Diamond next door hosts the Round Rock Express, the Triple-A affiliate that Nolan Ryan brought to town in 2000.

name: Onion Creek Metropolitan Park
story: 393 acres in southeast Austin along Onion Creek, largely undeveloped floodplain and trail.
extra: Much of the land was bought out by the city after repeated catastrophic flooding, most severely in 2013 and 2015.

name: Patterson Neighborhood Park
story: Nine acres in the Cherrywood area off Wilshire, with tennis courts and a creek trail.
extra: The park anchors Cherrywood, and its tennis courts have hosted a neighbourhood league that has run continuously since the 1970s.

name: Pease District Park
story: Forty acres along Shoal Creek west of downtown, running north from 15th Street. Given to the city by the family of Governor Elisha Pease.
extra: Eeyore's Birthday Party has been held here every April since 1963, a drum circle and costume gathering that started as a UT English department picnic.

name: Quail Creek Neighborhood Park
story: Sixteen acres in north Austin off Rundberg Lane.
extra: The park serves one of the densest apartment corridors in north Austin, and its pool is among the busiest free pools in the city each summer.

name: Ramsey Park
story: Five acres in Rosedale off Burnet Road, with a pool and tennis courts.
extra: The pool here is one of a handful of Austin neighbourhood pools old enough to have been segregated by law, and its integration in the 1960s was fought block by block.

name: Republic Square
story: One of the four squares in Austin's 1839 plan, at Fourth and Guadalupe. Rebuilt in 2017 around the live oaks that survived a century of parking lots.
extra: The oldest tree here predates the city. The square was Mexican American Austin's social center in the 19th century before the neighborhood was pushed east.

name: Roy G. Guerrero Park
story: 437 acres along the Colorado River in southeast Austin, one of the largest parks in the city, with disc golf, trails, and a secret beach on the river.
extra: Named for a longtime city parks employee. The 'secret beach' is a sand bar on the river that stopped being secret about a decade ago.

name: Seiders Springs Park
story: Six acres along Shoal Creek north of 38th Street, named for the springs that fed an early bathhouse resort here.
extra: Edward Seiders ran a spa and picnic grounds at the springs in the 1870s. Stone steps from it are still visible on the creek bank.

name: Shipe Park
story: Three acres in Hyde Park at 44th and Avenue G, named for Monroe Shipe, who developed the neighborhood in the 1890s.
extra: Shipe ran the streetcar line that made Hyde Park viable, and he set this land aside as an amenity to sell lots.

name: Shoal Creek Greenbelt
story: A narrow corridor following Shoal Creek from Lady Bird Lake north past 38th Street, linking Pease Park to downtown.
extra: The 1981 Memorial Day flood sent water fifteen feet up these banks and killed thirteen people, which is why so much of the floodplain is parkland now.

name: Springdale Park
story: Fifteen acres in East Austin off Springdale Road, near the Govalle and Johnston Terrace neighborhoods.
extra: Springdale Road was a rural farm route until the 1950s, and the park preserves one of the last undeveloped stretches along it.

name: Tarrytown Neighborhood Park
story: Three acres in west Austin off Exposition, the neighborhood's park and playground.
extra: The park sits on land that was part of the Tarrytown subdivision platted in the 1930s, when this was the far western edge of the city.

name: Walnut Creek Metropolitan Park
story: 298 acres in north Austin off Lamar, with fifteen miles of mountain bike and hiking trail along Walnut Creek.
extra: The off-leash area is one of the largest in the city, and the trail network is where most Austin mountain bikers learn to ride.

name: Walter E. Long Metropolitan Park
story: 3,600 acres around Decker Lake in far east Austin, by area the largest park in the city system and still mostly undeveloped.
extra: The lake is a cooling reservoir for the Decker power plant, which is why it stays warm enough to fish year-round.

name: Waterloo Park
story: Twelve acres at the northeast corner of downtown, reopened in 2021 after a long rebuild that turned Waller Creek into the park's spine.
extra: Austin's oldest city park, dating to 1839. The Moody Amphitheater sits at its center now.

name: West Austin Neighborhood Park
story: Three and a half acres in Old West Austin near Clarksville, with a pool and ballfields.
extra: It sits at the edge of Clarksville, the freedom colony founded in 1871, and the park's ballfields were a gathering point for that community for decades.

name: Wild Basin Wilderness Preserve
story: 408 acres of Hill Country west of Austin off Loop 360, with trails through canyon and juniper. Run by St. Edward's University.
extra: It was saved from development in the 1970s by a group of local women who raised the money themselves, and is now a golden-cheeked warbler habitat.

name: Wooldridge Square Park
story: A two-acre square west of the Capitol, sunk into a natural bowl with a bandstand at the bottom. Another of the 1839 squares.
extra: The bowl shape made it Austin's default political rally site for a century. Every governor from the 1900s onward gave speeches from that bandstand.

name: Zilker Metropolitan Park
story: 351 acres between Barton Creek and Lady Bird Lake, donated to the city by Andrew Zilker in 1917. It holds Barton Springs Pool, the Botanical Garden, and the Great Lawn.
extra: Austin City Limits takes over the Great Lawn every October, and the Zilker Holiday Tree is strung from a 155-foot moonlight tower each December.

name: Bastrop
story: About 10,000 people 30 miles southeast on the Colorado River, one of the oldest towns in Texas, settled in 1832.
extra: The Lost Pines here are an isolated stand of loblolly pine, separated from the East Texas pine belt by a hundred miles. The 2011 wildfire burned most of it; it is regrowing.

name: Bear Creek
story: About 400 people in southwest Travis County near Manchaca.
extra: One of the smallest incorporated places in Travis County, with under 400 residents. It incorporated in the 1980s to head off annexation.

name: Bee Cave
story: About 4,000 people west of Austin on TX 71, anchored by the Hill Country Galleria.
extra: Named for a cave of wild bees in a bluff above Barton Creek.

name: Briarcliff
story: About 850 people on the south shore of Lake Travis, west of Bee Cave.
extra: Willie Nelson's Pedernales Country Club and recording studio are here.

name: Buda
story: About 15,000 people on I-35 south of Austin in Hays County.
extra: Pronounced BYOO-da, not BOO-da. It hosts an annual wiener dog race that draws thousands.

name: Cedar Park
story: About 61,000 people northwest of Austin along US 183, grown from a rail stop into one of the fastest-expanding suburbs in Texas.
extra: The H-E-B Center hosts the Texas Stars, the AHL affiliate of the Dallas Stars.

name: Coupland
story: A small town in Williamson County northeast of Austin, on the old rail line toward Taylor.
extra: A Williamson County farm town on the old rail line, best known now for a dance hall in a 1904 building that still books touring acts.

name: Creedmoor
story: About 190 people southeast of Austin along US 183.
extra: Under 200 residents on US 183 southeast of Austin, and the smallest city in Travis County by population.

name: Dripping Springs
story: About 6,000 people 25 miles west in Hays County, in the Hill Country.
extra: It calls itself the Wedding Capital of Texas, and it was the first International Dark Sky Community in Texas.

name: Elgin
story: About 10,000 people 25 miles east on US 290, in both Bastrop and Travis counties.
extra: The Sausage Capital of Texas by legislative designation, with smokehouses that have been running since the 1880s.

name: Georgetown
story: The Williamson County seat, about 67,000 people 30 miles north. Its Victorian courthouse square is one of the best preserved in Texas.
extra: Sun City, the retirement community on its west side, is why Georgetown has repeatedly ranked among the fastest-growing cities in the country.

name: Hays
story: About 240 people in Hays County southwest of Buda, one of the smallest incorporated places in the metro.
extra: About 240 people, and one of the very few Texas cities that shares its name with the county it sits in.

name: Hutto
story: About 27,000 people east of Round Rock, a former cotton and rail town now absorbed into the metro.
extra: The town mascot is the hippo. The story goes that a circus hippo escaped into Cottonwood Creek in 1915, and there are now hundreds of hippo statues around town.

name: Jonestown
story: About 2,100 people on the north shore of Lake Travis.
extra: Named for the Jones brothers, who ran a pecan shelling operation here in the 1930s. No relation to the one in Guyana.

name: Kyle
story: About 28,000 people on I-35 between Austin and San Marcos, in Hays County.
extra: Named for Fergus Kyle, and the hometown of novelist Katherine Anne Porter, whose childhood house is a museum.

name: Lago Vista
story: About 6,000 people on the north shore of Lake Travis, northwest of Austin.
extra: Platted as a lakeside resort development in the 1960s, it still has more platted lots than houses, and its own small airport sits in the middle of town.

name: Lakeway
story: About 19,000 people on the south shore of Lake Travis, built around a golf resort in the 1960s.
extra: It began as a resort: three Houston businessmen bought a 2,700-acre ranch in 1962 and cut the ribbon on the Lakeway Inn in July 1963. Residents voted to incorporate in 1974.

name: Leander
story: About 27,000 people northwest of Austin at the end of the Capital Metro rail line.
extra: The Leanderthal Lady, a 10,000-year-old skeleton found here in 1983, is one of the oldest and most complete human remains ever found in North America.

name: Manor
story: About 14,000 people east of Austin on US 290.
extra: Pronounced MAY-ner. Parts of Friday Night Lights and Miss Congeniality were filmed here.

name: Mustang Ridge
story: About 900 people southeast of Austin along I-35, split across Travis, Caldwell and Bastrop counties.
extra: The city straddles three counties, Travis, Caldwell and Bastrop, which means its residents can vote in different county elections depending which side of town they live on.

name: Pflugerville
story: About 65,000 people directly northeast of Austin, settled by German immigrants in the 1860s and named for Henry Pfluger.
extra: The silent P trips up everyone who has not lived here. Locals lean into it: the high school teams are the Panthers, and the annual festival is the Pfestival.

name: Point Venture
story: A small village on a peninsula in Lake Travis, northwest of Austin.
extra: A village on a peninsula jutting into Lake Travis, so narrow that when the lake is full it is water on three sides.

name: Rollingwood
story: About 1,500 people just west of Zilker Park, a small city entirely surrounded by Austin and West Lake Hills.
extra: A city of about 1,500 completely surrounded by Austin and West Lake Hills. It incorporated in 1955, and its entire commercial tax base is a single strip along Bee Cave Road.

name: Round Rock
story: Austin's largest suburb at about 119,000 people, 20 miles north on I-35. Named for a round rock in Brushy Creek that marked a safe wagon crossing on the Chisholm Trail.
extra: Dell was founded here in 1984 and still anchors the local economy. Sam Bass, the outlaw, was fatally shot in a gunfight downtown in 1878.

name: San Leanna
story: About 500 people south of Austin off Manchaca Road, a small residential village.
extra: About 500 people in a single wooded subdivision off Manchaca Road. It incorporated in 1971 and has no commercial district at all.

name: Sunset Valley
story: About 700 people, a small city entirely surrounded by Austin near Brodie Lane and US 290.
extra: It incorporated in 1954 specifically to avoid annexation by Austin, and funds itself largely through sales tax from the shopping centers inside its limits.

name: Taylor
story: About 16,000 people 35 miles northeast in Williamson County, a cotton and rail town.
extra: Samsung is building a semiconductor fabrication plant here, one of the largest single investments in Texas history.

name: The Hills
story: A small village on Lake Travis near Lakeway, built around a golf course.
extra: A village built around the Hills Country Club golf course, incorporated in 1980. Nearly every property line in it touches a fairway or a green.

name: Volente
story: About 400 people on the north shore of Lake Travis, northwest of Austin.
extra: Volente Beach, the lakeside waterpark, is the main reason anyone outside the area knows the name.

name: Webberville
story: About 400 people east of Austin on the Colorado River.
extra: Named for John Webber, a white settler who married a formerly enslaved woman, Silvia, and founded a community here in the 1830s before racial hostility drove them to Mexico.

name: Wells Branch
story: An unincorporated community between Austin and Pflugerville, one of the largest municipal utility districts in the state.
extra: Not a city at all: it is one of the largest municipal utility districts in Texas, an unincorporated area of about 12,000 people that runs its own parks and library.

name: West Lake Hills
story: About 3,400 people immediately west of Austin across the river, one of the wealthiest municipalities in Texas.
extra: It incorporated in 1953 largely to keep Austin from annexing it, and its hillside lots and limited commercial zoning have kept the population near 3,000 ever since.

name: ACL Live at the Moody Theater
story: A 2,750-seat theatre in the Second Street District, opened in 2011 as the permanent home of Austin City Limits.
extra: Austin City Limits is the longest-running music programme in American television history, on the air since 1974. It taped at a KLRU studio on the UT campus for 36 years before moving here.

name: Barton Creek Square Mall
story: A hillside shopping mall off Loop 360 in southwest Austin, opened in 1981.
extra: It was built into the slope, so the parking decks step down the hillside and the main level sits above the treeline with a view back toward downtown.

name: Bob Bullock IMAX Theatre
story: The IMAX screen inside the Bullock Texas State History Museum, six storeys high and 84 feet wide, the largest in Texas.
extra: It is one of only a handful of theatres in the world running IMAX dual-laser projection, and it keeps its own entrance so it can stay open after the museum closes.

name: Circuit of the Americas
story: A 3.4-mile FIA Grade 1 racetrack southeast of Austin, opened in 2012 as the first purpose-built Formula One circuit in the United States. It hosts the US Grand Prix, MotoGP, and NASCAR.
extra: Turn 1 climbs 133 feet at a gradient steeper than any corner in Formula One. The 251-foot observation tower is visible from the highway.

name: Comedy Mothership
story: A comedy club on Sixth Street in the former Ritz theatre building, opened in 2023 by Joe Rogan.
extra: The Ritz opened in 1929 as Austin's first theatre built for talkies, and was an Alamo Drafthouse for years before this.

name: Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium
story: Home to Longhorns football since 1924, seating 100,119, the seventh-largest stadium in the United States.
extra: The name has no period after the K because the K does not stand for anything. Royal coached the team to three national titles and the stadium was renamed for him while he was still alive.

name: Dell Diamond
story: The 11,000-seat ballpark in Round Rock, home to the Round Rock Express since 2000.
extra: Nolan Ryan brought the team to town and his family ran it for years. The Express are the Triple-A affiliate of the Texas Rangers.

name: Emo's
story: A music venue in south Austin off Riverside, holding about 1,700.
extra: The original Emo's on Red River was the centre of Austin's punk scene through the 1990s. It moved out here in 2011, and the name still carries more weight than the building.

name: Empire Control Room & Garage
story: A 15,000-square-foot venue at Seventh and Red River with three stages: an indoor control room, an outdoor garage, and a creekside patio.
extra: The garage stage really was an auto body shop, and at 1,050 capacity it is the largest of the three rooms.

name: Gregory Gymnasium
story: The historic gymnasium at the centre of the UT campus, opened in 1930 and still the main student recreation building.
extra: Longhorns basketball played here for half a century before the Erwin Center. Its outdoor pool is one of the few places on campus open year-round.

name: H-E-B Center at Cedar Park
story: An 8,700-seat arena in Cedar Park, opened in 2009, home to the Texas Stars hockey team.
extra: The Stars are the AHL affiliate of the Dallas Stars, which makes this the only place in Central Texas to watch professional hockey.

name: Hamilton Pool Preserve
story: A collapsed grotto west of Austin where Hamilton Creek drops fifty feet into a jade green pool below a limestone overhang.
extra: The dome collapsed thousands of years ago. Travis County now caps daily visitors by reservation, and swimming is closed whenever bacteria counts run high.

name: Hill Country Galleria
story: An open-air shopping centre in Bee Cave on TX 71, opened in 2007 and built around a central green.
extra: Bee Cave city hall and the public library sit inside the development, which makes it one of the few Texas malls that is also a civic centre.

name: IKEA Round Rock
story: The Central Texas IKEA on I-35 in Round Rock, opened in 2006, about 250,000 square feet.
extra: It was the first IKEA in Texas outside the Dallas area, and for years Austinites drove to Round Rock rather than Houston or Frisco for flat-pack furniture.

name: Inner Space Cavern
story: A cave under I-35 in Georgetown, discovered in 1963 when a highway department core drill broke through the ceiling.
extra: Bones found inside included mammoth, sabre-toothed cat and giant sloth that had fallen through natural entrances that later sealed shut, some more than 20,000 years old.

name: Krieg Field
story: A 56-acre softball complex on Pleasant Valley beside the Colorado River, with seven lit fields. It is the centre of adult league softball in Austin.
extra: It sits on the floodplain, so the fields go under water when the river rises, and league play has been rained out for whole seasons.

name: Lakeline Mall
story: A shopping mall in far northwest Austin near Cedar Park, opened in October 1995.
extra: Construction stalled twice: first in the savings and loan crisis, then again when two endangered species turned up on the site. It opened with hot air balloons that shot fake flames on a timer.

name: Mike A. Myers Stadium
story: UT's track and soccer stadium, just north of DKR, seating about 20,000.
extra: It has hosted the Texas Relays since 1999, one of the largest track meets in the country, which draws tens of thousands of athletes and spectators to Austin every spring.

name: Moody Amphitheater
story: A 5,000-capacity outdoor amphitheatre in Waterloo Park, opened in 2021 as part of the park's rebuild.
extra: It sits over Waller Creek, which was rerouted and daylighted underneath during construction.

name: Moody Center
story: A 15,000-seat arena on the UT campus, opened in 2022 to replace the Frank Erwin Center. Home court for Longhorns basketball and a regular tour stop.
extra: It was built on a former parking lot. In its first full year it outsold every other arena its size in the world by ticket revenue.

name: Nelson Field
story: An Austin ISD football stadium in northeast Austin, off US 290.
extra: It is one of two district stadiums that host most Austin public high school football, which means on a Friday night in autumn it is one of the busiest places in the city.

name: Palmer Events Center
story: A 130,000-square-foot event hall on Auditorium Shores, opened in 2002.
extra: It replaced the Palmer Auditorium, a domed 1959 building on the same site whose shell was reused as the Long Center next door.

name: Paramount Theatre
story: A 1915 classical revival theater on Congress Avenue, still running as a live venue and movie house. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1976.
extra: It opened as the Majestic on the vaudeville circuit. Harry Houdini and the Marx Brothers both played the stage before it became a cinema.

name: Parker Jazz Club
story: A basement jazz room at Fourth and Colorado in the Warehouse District, opened in 2018.
extra: It is one of very few rooms in Austin built specifically for jazz, lit by candlelight and run as a listening room rather than a bar with a band.

name: Q2 Stadium
story: A 20,500-seat soccer-specific stadium in North Burnet, home to Austin FC since the club began play in 2021.
extra: Its first event was not an Austin FC match but a friendly between the US women's national team and Nigeria in June 2021. The supporters' section behind the north goal is loud enough that visiting coaches complain about it on the record.

name: Round Rock Premium Outlets
story: An outlet mall on I-35 in Round Rock with about 125 stores, opened in 2006.
extra: It draws shoppers from as far as Mexico on holiday weekends, and the traffic it generates is a standing item at Round Rock council meetings.

name: State Theatre
story: A 1935 theatre on Congress Avenue, next door to the Paramount and operated with it.
extra: It closed in 2005 after structural problems and sat dark for more than a decade before reopening in 2021.

name: Stubb's Waller Creek Amphitheater
story: An outdoor amphitheatre behind Stubb's Bar-B-Q on Red River, holding about 2,200.
extra: The building dates to 1851 and is one of the oldest structures in Austin. C.B. Stubblefield moved his Lubbock barbecue operation here in 1996.

name: The Domain
story: A dense mix of offices, shops, and apartments in northwest Austin, opened in 2007 and often called Austin's second downtown.
extra: It sits on land that was an IBM campus. The nickname is only half a joke: it now has more office space than many actual downtowns in Texas.

name: The Hideout Theatre
story: An improv theatre and coffeehouse on Congress Avenue downtown.
notes: Left 617 Congress in 2026; OSM point is the old address, now becoming a bar. Re-add at 5555 N Lamar if wanted.

name: Whitaker Intramural Fields
story: UT's intramural fields on the east side of campus, about 60 acres of pitches.
extra: Named for Chuck Whitaker, a longtime UT recreational sports director. The fields sit on land that was a municipal golf course before the university acquired it.
